science.s: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
science.e: Lightning often strikes tall objects repeatedly. The Empire State Building is hit around 20 to 25 times a year.

science.s: Water expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats.
science.e: As water freezes, its molecules form an open hexagonal lattice that takes up about 9% more space. Lakes freeze from the top down, which protects the life below.

science.s: Old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows downward over centuries.
science.e: Glass at room temperature doesn't flow measurably. Old panes were uneven because of how they were made, and glaziers often put the thicker edge at the bottom.

science.s: Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.
science.e: Sound moves at about 343 m/s in air and roughly 1,480 m/s in water, because water's molecules are packed much more closely.

science.s: Helium is the only element that won't freeze solid at normal pressure, no matter how cold it gets.
science.e: Even near absolute zero, helium stays liquid unless it's squeezed to about 25 times atmospheric pressure.

science.s: Early humans lived alongside the dinosaurs.
science.e: Non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. Our species appeared only about 300,000 years ago. Birds, however, are living dinosaurs.

science.s: Diamonds and the graphite in pencils are made of the same element.
science.e: Both are pure carbon. In diamond the atoms form a rigid 3D lattice. In graphite they form sheets that slide over each other.

science.s: The Eiffel Tower can grow about 15 cm taller in summer.
science.e: Iron expands when it heats up, so the tower's height varies by around 15 cm with the temperature.

science.s: Absolute zero, −273.15 °C, is the lowest temperature possible.
science.e: At absolute zero, particles would have the minimum possible energy. Scientists have cooled atoms to within billionths of a degree of it, but never reached it.

science.s: Different areas of the tongue detect different tastes: sweet at the tip, bitter at the back.
science.e: The 'tongue map' came from a mistranslation of a 1901 German paper. Every area of the tongue that has taste buds can detect all basic tastes.

science.s: The air we breathe is mostly oxygen.
science.e: Earth's atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and only about 21% oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide and other gases making up the rest.

science.s: A lightning bolt can be about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
science.e: Lightning can heat the air to around 30,000 °C, while the Sun's visible surface is about 5,500 °C.

science.s: Water can boil at room temperature if the air pressure is low enough.
science.e: A liquid's boiling point drops with pressure. That's why water boils at around 70 °C on top of Mount Everest.

science.s: Albert Einstein failed mathematics at school.
science.e: This is a popular myth. Einstein excelled at maths and had mastered calculus by about age 15.

science.s: Antibiotics are effective against the viruses that cause colds and flu.
science.e: Antibiotics only work against bacteria. Using them for viral infections doesn't help and contributes to antibiotic resistance.

space.s: A day on Venus is longer than its year.
space.e: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once, but only about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun. It also spins backwards compared with most planets.

space.s: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
space.e: The Sun is about 150 million km away. If it suddenly vanished, we wouldn't notice for about 8 minutes.

space.s: There is no gravity on the International Space Station.
space.e: Gravity at the ISS's height is about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they're in constant free fall around Earth.

space.s: The footprints left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts could last for millions of years.
space.e: The Moon has no wind or water to erase them. Only slow erosion from tiny meteorite impacts will eventually wear them away.

space.s: Saturn is less dense than water.
space.e: Saturn's average density is about 0.69 g/cm³, lower than water's 1 g/cm³. In a big enough bathtub, it would float.

space.s: Olympus Mons on Mars is about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.
space.e: This shield volcano rises about 22 km and is roughly as wide as France. It's one of the largest volcanoes in the Solar System.

space.s: Seen from space, the Sun is yellow.
space.e: The Sun emits all visible colours and appears white from space. It looks yellow from Earth because our atmosphere scatters the blue light.

space.s: Some neutron stars spin hundreds of times per second.
space.e: Neutron stars are city-sized remains of exploded stars. The fastest known spins about 716 times a second.

space.s: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm that has been observed for nearly 200 years.
space.e: It has been observed continuously since at least 1831. The storm is wider than Earth, though it has been shrinking.

space.s: In 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 became the first mission to land near the Moon's south pole.
space.e: Its Vikram lander touched down on 23 August 2023, a region of interest because it may contain water ice.

space.s: Mercury is the hottest planet because it's closest to the Sun.
space.e: Venus is the hottest planet, at about 465 °C, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat. Mercury has almost no atmosphere and is freezing on its night side.

space.s: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object.
space.e: It entered interstellar space in 2012 and is now more than 24 billion km away. Its signals take over 22 hours to reach us.

space.s: More than a million Earths could fit inside the Sun.
space.e: The Sun's volume is about 1.3 million times Earth's. It holds 99.8% of the mass in the Solar System.

space.s: Astronauts can grow slightly taller while living in space.
space.e: Without gravity compressing the spine, astronauts can grow up to about 3% taller. They shrink back after returning to Earth.
space.w: Effect of spaceflight on the human body

space.s: The first person in space was Yuri Gagarin, in 1961.
space.e: On 12 April 1961 he orbited Earth once in Vostok 1, a flight of 108 minutes.

body.s: Humans use only 10% of their brains.
body.e: Brain scans show activity throughout the brain, and almost every area has a known function. Even during sleep, many areas stay active.
body.w: Ten percent of the brain myth

body.s: Babies are born with more bones than adults have.
body.e: Newborns have around 270 to 300 bones. Many fuse together during growth, leaving adults with 206.

body.s: The cells lining your stomach are replaced every few days.
body.e: The stomach's surface cells are constantly renewed, and a layer of mucus protects them from the strong acid that digests food.

body.s: Hair and fingernails keep growing after death.
body.e: After death the skin dries and pulls back, which makes hair and nails look longer. Growth needs living cells and stops.

body.s: Most stomach ulcers are caused by a bacterium, not by stress.
body.e: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed that Helicobacter pylori causes most ulcers. Marshall even drank a culture of it, and they won the 2005 Nobel Prize.

body.s: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
body.e: At around 70 beats per minute, that's roughly 100,000 beats a day and nearly 3 billion over a lifetime.
Studies have found no link. One doctor cracked the knuckles of only one hand for over 60 years and found no difference between his hands.

body.s: The smallest bone in the human body is in the ear.
body.e: The stapes, or stirrup, in the middle ear is about 3 mm long. It passes sound vibrations to the inner ear.

body.s: Blood in your veins is blue until it touches oxygen.
body.e: Blood is always red: bright red when oxygen-rich and darker red when not. Veins look blue because of how light passes through skin.

body.s: The cornea of your eye has no blood vessels and gets much of its oxygen directly from the air.
body.e: Blood vessels would block your vision, so the cornea absorbs oxygen dissolved in the tear film from the air.

body.s: Even identical twins have different fingerprints.
body.e: Fingerprints form in the womb, shaped by genes and by tiny differences in pressure, position and the surrounding fluid.

body.s: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker and darker.
body.e: Shaving cuts hair at a blunt angle, which can feel coarser, but it doesn't change thickness, colour or growth rate.

body.s: The human liver can regrow after a large part of it is removed.
body.e: The liver can regenerate to its full size even after much of it is removed, which makes living-donor liver transplants possible.

body.s: You lose most of your body heat through your head.
body.e: The head loses heat at about the same rate as any other uncovered part of the body. The myth came from a flawed military experiment.

nature.s: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
nature.e: Two hearts pump blood to the gills and one to the rest of the body. Their blood uses copper-based haemocyanin, which makes it blue.

nature.s: Bulls charge because the colour red makes them angry.
nature.e: Cattle can't distinguish red from green well. Bulls react to the movement of the cape, not its colour.

nature.s: A group of flamingos is called a 'flamboyance'.
nature.e: Flamingos get their pink colour from pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat.

nature.s: Goldfish have a memory of only three seconds.
nature.e: Experiments show goldfish can remember things for months, and they can be trained to respond to sounds, colours and lights.

nature.s: One jellyfish species can turn back into an earlier stage of its life, making it biologically 'immortal'.
nature.e: When stressed or injured, Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from adult to polyp and start its life cycle again.

nature.s: Sea otters often hold paws while they sleep so they don't drift apart.
nature.e: Sea otters rest floating on their backs, often in groups called rafts, and may wrap themselves in kelp to stay anchored.
The cubes form in the last part of the wombat's intestine. Wombats use them to mark territory, and the flat sides stop them rolling away.
All bats can see, and many see well. Many species also use echolocation to hunt in the dark.

nature.s: Tardigrades, or 'water bears', can survive exposure to the vacuum of space.
nature.e: In 2007, tardigrades survived 10 days exposed to space. They can enter a dried-out state that withstands extreme cold, heat and radiation.

nature.s: Some species of bamboo can grow almost a metre in a single day.
nature.e: Some bamboos grow up to about 91 cm in 24 hours, among the fastest growth of any plant.

nature.s: Ostriches bury their heads in the sand when they're scared.
nature.e: Ostriches don't do this. They lie low or run at up to 70 km/h. The myth may come from them turning their eggs in nests dug into the ground.

nature.s: A blue whale's heart can weigh around 180 kg.
nature.e: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, and its heartbeat can be detected from kilometres away.

nature.s: Koalas spend up to about 20 hours a day sleeping or resting.
nature.e: Their eucalyptus diet is low in nutrients and energy, so they save energy by resting most of the day.

nature.s: The Amazon rainforest is home to around 10% of all known species on Earth.
nature.e: It's the world's largest tropical rainforest, spread across nine countries, and new species are discovered there every year.

nature.s: Honeybees tell each other where to find flowers by dancing.
nature.e: In the 'waggle dance', the angle of the dance shows the direction relative to the Sun and its length shows the distance.

nature.s: In seahorses, the males carry the eggs and give birth.
nature.e: The female places her eggs in the male's pouch, where he fertilises and carries them until hundreds of tiny seahorses are born.

mind.s: People who are bad at something tend to overestimate how good they are at it.
mind.e: This is known as the Dunning–Kruger effect: a lack of skill can also mean a lack of the knowledge needed to judge that skill.
Some functions are stronger on one side, but large studies find no evidence that people rely on one hemisphere more than the other.

mind.s: Seeing faces in clouds, cars or electrical sockets has a name: pareidolia.
mind.e: Our brains are tuned to detect faces quickly, so they often find them where none exist.

mind.s: Students learn much better when teaching matches their 'learning style' (visual, auditory or kinesthetic).
mind.e: People have preferences, but studies have found little evidence that matching teaching to a 'learning style' improves results.

mind.s: You remember things better if you spread your study sessions out over time.
mind.e: This is called the spacing effect. Reviewing material across several days beats cramming. This app brings back facts you got wrong for the same reason.

mind.s: Most people can hold only around 4 to 7 items in short-term memory at once.
mind.e: That's why phone numbers are split into chunks: grouping information helps memory hold more.

mind.s: After you learn a new word, it suddenly seems to appear everywhere. This feeling has a name.
mind.e: It's called the frequency illusion, or Baader–Meinhof phenomenon. Your attention now notices something that was always there.
Controlled studies have found no effect of sugar on children's behaviour. Parents who believe their child had sugar tend to rate them as more hyperactive.

mind.s: People are less likely to help someone in trouble when other bystanders are present.
mind.e: This is the bystander effect: responsibility feels shared, so each person waits for someone else to act.

mind.s: The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy.
mind.e: The brain's roughly 86 billion neurons are constantly active, which makes it the most energy-hungry organ for its size.

mind.s: A placebo can help some patients even when they know it's a placebo.
mind.e: Studies of 'open-label' placebos found that some patients, for example with irritable bowel syndrome, reported improvement even after being told the pills were fake.

mind.s: Playing Mozart to babies makes them more intelligent.
mind.e: The 'Mozart effect' study found only a brief, small boost on one kind of puzzle in college students. Later studies did not find lasting effects.
